sources.news_title: US mother to face retrial over children's deaths
sources.text:
The US mother accused of killing her three children will face a retrial starting March 29, a judge ruled on Monday, after a jury deadlocked in a case that has gripped the nation.
Lindsay Clancy, 36, did not deny at her first trial that she strangled her kids Cora, age five, Dawson, three, and Callan, eight months. She claimed she was suffering from postpartum psychosis – which she said excuses her from criminal responsibility.
In September a jury of nine women and three men failed to reach a unanimous decision, as required in US criminal proceedings, causing a mistrial.
Clancy's original trial, which featured more than 80 witnesses and days of distressing testimony, sparked debate in the United States over maternal mental health.
She pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity and said she heard a voice ordering her to kill her children. Her lawyers said this was caused by postpartum psychosis, a condition that medical experts say affects about one to two women in every 1,000 births.
Prosecutors rejected that argument, saying Clancy had carefully planned the murders and was able to understand the consequences of her actions.
After the killings at the family home in Duxbury, Massachusetts, in January 2023, Clancy cut her neck and wrists and jumped from a second-story window in an apparent suicide attempt that has left her paralysed from the waist down and confined to a wheelchair.
"Why don't we put it (retrial) on for March 29," when jury selection will begin, said Massachusetts state Judge William Sullivan in a short hearing on Monday.
Clancy will return to court on December 30 for a status update in the case, according to a court official.
Kevin Reddington, who is defending Clancy, previously asked the judge to enter a not-guilty verdict, essentially dismissing the case after the weeks-long, televised trial that captivated Americans.

Instead, the judge opted for a retrial after a number of hearings at which the prosecution and defence did battle over Clancy's fate.
"Where is the evidence she did this?" said Reddington previously. He also cast doubt on Clancy's own admissions that she killed her children. (AFP)

sources.news_title: Lindsay Clancy to face retrial in March
sources.text:
Lindsay Clancy, accused of murdering her three young children, will face retrial on March 29, 2027.
Her first trial ended in a mistrial after jurors were unable to reach a unanimous verdict on whether she was criminally responsible for the killings.
Attorneys are scheduled to return to court on December 30 to discuss trial logistics, security and media arrangements.
A Massachusetts judge has scheduled Lindsay Clancy's retrial for late March after prosecutors signalled that — at least for now — they intended to prosecute her again on first-degree murder charges in the killings of her three young children.
Ms Clancy's first trial ended in a mistrial after jurors were unable to reach a unanimous verdict on whether she was criminally responsible for the killings.
Eleven jurors favoured acquittal on the grounds of insanity, while one disagreed.
While the Plymouth County district attorney has not indicated publicly whether his office will pursue the same charges in a second trial, Assistant District Attorney Jennifer Sprague told the judge during Monday's hearing that prosecutors were "ready to pick a jury trial date".
Ms Clancy's lawyer, Kevin Reddington, said he took that to mean prosecutors intended to go ahead with a first-degree murder case, as a lesser charge would allow Clancy to waive her right to have a jury.
"The die has been cast," Mr Reddington told Judge William Sullivan.
"I think you can read between the lines that when they say that the case is going to require a jury, that it's an indirect comment from the DA that they intend to proceed on first-degree murder indictments."
Prosecutors had sought a May trial date, citing scheduling conflicts, but Judge Sullivan set the retrial for March 29.
The decision to schedule Ms Clancy's second trial comes a week after Judge Sullivan rejected a defence request to dismiss the charges.
He ruled that a retrial would not violate Ms Clancy's constitutional protection against double jeopardy.
Attorneys are scheduled to return to court on December 30 to discuss trial logistics, security and media arrangements.
Ms Clancy, a former labour and delivery nurse, has never disputed that she killed her three children at the family's Duxbury home in January 2023.
Her attorneys said she was suffering from postpartum psychosis, a rare mental illness that can afflict mothers after childbirth.
Prosecutors argued Ms Clancy planned the killings and understood what she was doing.

Lindsay Clancy's new trial for the killings of her 3 children has been set
A Massachusetts judge revealed in court Monday morning the date that Lindsay Clancy's new trial will take place.
Lindsay Clancy's new trial for the killings of her three children has been set.
Judge William Sullivan said in court Monday morning that the trial will take place March 29, ABC News reported.
'The die has been cast.'
The Plymouth County District Attorney's Office did not say on what charges Clancy would be retried, but Jennifer Sprague — one of the prosecutors — said it would require a jury, the news network noted.
The defense said that points to prosecutors intending to retry Clancy on first-degree murder charges given that lesser charges could result in a bench trial, ABC News said.
"I think from the Commonwealth's perspective, given what the charges are, it requires a jury trial," Sprague said, according to the news network. "We haven't heard from defense counsel about any other direction for the trial. So without that, we'd be ready to pick a trial date."
ABC News added that defense attorney Kevin Reddington stated that "the die has been cast. I think you can read between the lines that when they say that the case is going to require a jury ... it's an indirect comment from the DA that they intend to proceed on first-degree murder indictments."
Prosecutors earlier this month said they wanted Clancy to stand trial again — but it wasn't clear then, either, what charges Clancy would face at a retrial, WBZ-TV reported.
Reddington in Clancy's first trial acknowledged that she killed her children — 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson, and 8-month-old Callan — in their Duxbury, Massachusetts, home in January 2023, WBZ said.
But Clancy pleaded not guilty to first-degree murder, and Reddington argued that his client wasn't criminally responsible because she was overmedicated and suffering from postpartum psychosis, the station added.
Prosecutors disagreed, saying Clancy knew right from wrong and planned to strangle her children, WBZ said.
The prosecution also maintained that Clancy schemed to get her husband out of the house that evening her children were killed by sending him to pick up medicine for one of their children and dinner for the family, the Associated Press said.
The first trial ended Sept. 4 with a hung jury; one juror held out, believing Clancy was guilty, while the other 11 believed she was not guilty of murder.
Judge Sullivan earlier this month told the prosecution and defense that he wanted a new trial to begin sometime in March, ABC News said, adding that part of the reason is that he'll be nearing his mandatory retirement age for Massachusetts judges later this year.
"I'm thinking sometime in March if we can do that, or earlier if possible," Sullivan said, according to the news network. "But I think March is probably realistic."
Reddington also said he wanted a spring trial date, ABC News reported: "I am not going to have this woman sit incarcerated for the next year or two or three. I want a trial, and I want it with you, and I want it this spring."
According to the news network, Sprague said that it "would be a retrial. As to what that looks like will depend. We're not at that point yet. I think once we get the decision on the motions and see what happens from there, then we would decide what that looks like. But it would be a retrial."
More from ABC News:
Defense lawyers took aim at that holdout juror over the last two months, pushing the court to investigate whether the juror followed the court's instructions and asking the court to throw out the case based on their argument that the judge failed to adequately question the holdout about whether he was following the reasonable-doubt instruction during the final days of deliberations.
Sullivan rejected both of those motions, ABC News said, as well as the prosecution's request for a gag order ahead of a potential retrial.
"Because the Court concludes that there was a manifest necessity for a mistrial based on the jury's deadlock, a retrial on the murder indictments does not violate Clancy's right not to be placed in double jeopardy," Judge Sullivan wrote, according to the news network.
Clancy's defense team said they plan to appeal that ruling but promised their appeal would not delay a retrial, ABC News added.

sources.news_title: Massachusetts Judge Schedules Lindsay Clancy Murder Retrial for March 29 Despite Prosecutors’ Objections
sources.text:
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom
A Massachusetts judge on Monday, Nov. 16, scheduled Lindsay Clancy’s second murder trial for March 29, 2027, rejecting prosecutors’ request for additional preparation time after her first trial ended with 11 jurors favoring an insanity acquittal and one juror opposing it.
Plymouth Superior Court Judge William Sullivan established the new trial date during a hearing in Plymouth, Massachusetts, where prosecutors indicated they intend to pursue the same three first-degree murder charges arising from the January 2023 deaths of Clancy’s children at the family’s Duxbury home.
According to Reuters’ coverage of Monday’s hearing, prosecutors sought a trial date in May or later, citing scheduling conflicts and the additional time required to prepare. Sullivan instead selected March 29, partly because he plans to retire in June and wants to oversee the proceedings himself.
Clancy, 36, is charged with killing her three children: Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and Callan, 8 months old. She has acknowledged causing their deaths, but her defense maintains that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis and was not criminally responsible for her actions.
The first trial ended Sept. 4 when the 12-member jury was unable to reach a unanimous verdict. Eleven jurors supported finding Clancy not guilty by reason of insanity, while one juror disagreed.
The deadlock prompted Sullivan to declare a mistrial, leaving prosecutors to determine whether to pursue another trial on the original charges or consider lesser offenses.
During Monday’s hearing, prosecutors indicated they would continue seeking first-degree murder convictions rather than reduce the charges. A conviction on those charges carries a mandatory sentence of life imprisonment without the possibility of parole.
The decision follows Sullivan’s Nov. 9 ruling rejecting the defense team’s attempt to dismiss the murder indictments on constitutional grounds.
Clancy’s attorneys argued that another trial would violate her Fifth Amendment protection against double jeopardy because the judge had declared a mistrial without sufficiently investigating the lone juror who opposed acquittal.
Sullivan disagreed, concluding that the jury’s inability to reach a verdict created the legal necessity for a mistrial.
“Because the Court concludes that there was a manifest necessity for a mistrial based on the jury’s deadlock, a retrial on the murder indictments does not violate Clancy’s right not to be placed in double jeopardy,” Sullivan wrote in his Nov. 9 ruling reported by ABC News.
The judge also denied requests to question the holdout juror and obtain records related to the individual’s participation in deliberations, citing concerns about juror privacy and the integrity of the deliberation process.
Clancy’s defense has maintained that severe postpartum psychiatric symptoms prevented her from understanding the wrongfulness of her conduct when she killed her children.
Her attorneys presented evidence during the first trial concerning her mental health treatment and psychiatric medications. Prosecutors argued that Clancy planned the killings and understood her actions, making her criminally responsible under Massachusetts law.
The case has attracted national attention because of its implications for postpartum mental illness and the legal standard for an insanity defense.
Under Massachusetts law, a defendant may be found not criminally responsible if a mental disease or defect substantially impaired the person’s ability to appreciate the criminality of their conduct or conform their behavior to the law.
Such a finding can result in commitment to a psychiatric facility rather than a prison sentence, with continued confinement subject to judicial review.
Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse, sustained severe injuries after attempting suicide following the deaths of her children. She remains paralyzed and has been held in custody while the criminal proceedings continue.
Her defense attorney, Kevin Reddington, has repeatedly argued against prolonged delays, emphasizing Clancy’s continued incarceration and the importance of resolving the case.
According to Associated Press reporting published Monday, Sullivan scheduled the retrial over prosecutors’ objections and established additional hearings to address preparations.
Attorneys are expected to return to court Dec. 30 to discuss logistical matters, including courtroom security and media arrangements. A pretrial conference is scheduled for Feb. 18.
The March 29 trial will again require jurors to determine whether Clancy was criminally responsible for the deaths of her children, with the prosecution pursuing first-degree murder convictions and the defense maintaining that her psychiatric condition prevented legal responsibility for the killings.

“I think from the Commonwealth’s perspective, given what the charges are, it requires a jury trial,” said Sprague. “We haven’t heard from defense counsel about any other direction for the trial. So without that, we’d be ready to pick a trial date.”
“Alea iacta est. The die has been cast. I think you can read between the lines that when they say that the case is going to require a jury, that it’s an indirect comment from the DA that they intend to proceed on first-degree murder indictments,” said defense attorney Kevin Reddington.
Most of Monday’s hearing was spent debating the best date to begin the trial, with prosecutors citing multiple conflicts for a spring trial.
“We can’t go tomorrow and tomorrow and tomorrow creeps upon its petty pace. We can’t do that. We’re going to pick a trial date,” said Sullivan.
The conference briefly got heated after prosecutors pushed back on a remark from Reddington about the trial aligning with the Ides of March, when Julius Caesar was assassinated.
“Sorry, I don’t have any jokes,” said Sprague.
“I’m not saying any jokes. All right, I’m just trying to talk to both counsel about getting a date,” Sullivan said.
This decision comes two months after nearly every juror rejected the murder case brought against Clancy, the Massachusetts mother accused of killing her three children.
Days earlier, Sullivan rejected Clancy’s main attempt to have the case thrown out.
“There’s all sorts of things we are waiting on, including judicial decisions, so we’ll take all our information, then we’re going to make a very methodical determination as to what we are going to do,” Cruz said outside court on Nov. 2. “I’ll be talking more on Nov. 16.”
“You think you’ll have a decision in two weeks?” a reporter asked.
“That’s my plan,” he said.
During a hearing earlier this month, Judge Sullivan told both sides that he would like the trial to begin sometime in March — in part because he is approaching the mandatory retirement age for judges in Massachusetts later this year.
“I’m thinking sometime in March if we can do that, or earlier if possible. But I think March is probably realistic,” Judge Sullivan said.
Reddington said he was in favor of a spring trial date as well, while expressing frustration that prosecutors have not yet announced how and if they plan to proceed with the case.
“I am not going to have this woman sit incarcerated for the next year or two or three. I want a trial, and I want it with you, and I want it this spring,” said Reddington.
“This would be a retrial,” said Assistant District Attorney Jennifer Sprague. “As to what that looks like will depend. We’re not at that point yet. I think once we get the decision on the motions and see what happens from there, then we would decide what that looks like. But it would be a retrial.”
Clancy’s initial trial ended in a hung jury after eleven jurors voted to acquit Clancy by reason of insanity, while one holdout juror forced a mistrial.
Defense lawyers took aim at that holdout juror over the last two months, pushing the court to investigate whether the juror followed the court’s instructions and asking the court to throw out the case based on their argument that the judge failed to adequately question the holdout about whether he was following the reasonable-doubt instruction during the final days of deliberations.
Judge Sullivan rejected both those motions last week, as well as the prosecution’s request for a gag order ahead of a potential retrial.
“Because the Court concludes that there was a manifest necessity for a mistrial based on the jury’s deadlock, a retrial on the murder indictments does not violate Clancy’s right not to be placed in double jeopardy,” Judge Sullivan wrote.
Clancy’s defense team said they plan to appeal that ruling but vowed that their appeal would not delay a retrial.

A Massachusetts judge announced on Monday that a new trial would begin on March 29 to determine whether Lindsay Clancy murdered her three children in 2023. That said, prosecutors’ agreement to another trial suggests they will pursue first-degree murder charges since, the Times reports, a judge could have ruled on second-degree murder or manslaughter charges without a trial.
The previous trial ended with 11 jurors wanting to acquit Clancy for the deaths of her children — Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and 8-month-old Callan — and one man, Michael P. Desronvil, insisting she was guilty. Another juror described him as “very arrogant” and claimed he had admitted he had reasonable doubts about her guilt. He disagreed with that claim. “Based on all the physical evidence, key witnesses and what the prosecution presented, I thought it was enough proof that she knew exactly what she was doing and planned,” he said in a September statement.
Since the mistrial, a GoFundMe campaign benefiting Clancy’s parents quickly raised more than $1.1 million since their lives were “put on hold.” Clancy’s lawyer, Kevin Reddington, also petitioned President Trump to pardon his client. Reddington, who sees another trial as double jeopardy, has said he feels it’s cruel to put Clancy through another trial.
Clancy remains in custody at a state hospital, according to the Times. Her lawyer had argued that she was experiencing postpartum depression and had hallucinated a voice that told her to strangle her children and kill herself. The case’s next hearing is scheduled for Dec. 30.

Lindsay Clancy is headed back to trial after her first jury split 11–1 in the deaths of her three children. A Massachusetts judge set jury selection for March 29, 2027, moving the case forward sooner than prosecutors had requested. Judge William Sullivan set the date during a brief hearing on Monday, November 16, in Plymouth Superior Court. Lindsay Clancy faces three counts of first-degree murder in the January 2023 deaths of Cora, Dawson and Callan Clancy. Her attorneys have argued that she was experiencing postpartum psychosis and should be found not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility.
The Judge Set A March Date Over Prosecutors’ Objections
Assistant District Attorney Jennifer Sprague asked to start the trial in May, citing scheduling conflicts. Sullivan instead set jury selection for late March and put two more court appearances on the calendar. The attorneys are due back on December 30 to discuss logistics, security and media arrangements. A final pretrial conference is set for February 18.
Prosecutors said Monday they were pursuing another jury trial. Defense attorney Kevin Reddington said he took that as a sign they would again pursue first-degree murder. Those charges remain pending, and prosecutors gave no indication at the hearing that they planned to proceed on lesser charges.
Why The First Jury’s 11–1 Split Led To A Mistrial
Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial on September 4 after jurors told the court they could not reach a unanimous verdict. Jurors who spoke publicly afterward said 11 members of the panel favored finding Lindsay Clancy not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility. One juror disagreed, leaving the case without a verdict.
Clancy’s lawyers later asked Judge William Sullivan to dismiss the charges. They argued that he should have investigated or removed the lone holdout before declaring a mistrial and that a second trial would violate Clancy’s constitutional protection against double jeopardy. Sullivan rejected that argument on November 9, clearing the way for Monday’s scheduling hearing.
What Happened At The Clancy Home In Duxbury
Lindsay Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse, does not dispute that she strangled her three children with exercise bands at the family’s Duxbury home on January 24, 2023. Cora was 5, and Dawson was 3. Both were taken to a hospital and later pronounced dead. Their infant brother, Callan, died several days later.
Authorities said Clancy jumped from a second-story window in an apparent suicide attempt after the killings. She survived with severe injuries that left her partially paralyzed. She uses a wheelchair and remains in custody at Tewksbury Hospital.
What The Two Sides Told Jurors About Her Mental State
At the first trial, the defense argued that postpartum psychosis left Lindsay Clancy unable to control her actions. Prosecutors argued that she planned the killings and understood what she was doing. Medical experts called by the prosecution testified that they found evidence of depression but concluded that she was not experiencing postpartum psychosis at the time.
The distinction carries major consequences. In Massachusetts, a first-degree murder conviction carries a mandatory sentence of life in prison without parole. A verdict of not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility can lead to commitment to a state psychiatric hospital, subject to court review.
What Happens Before The Next Jury Is Seated
The December hearing gives both sides a chance to work through arrangements for a case that drew national attention the first time around. The first trial involved more than 80 witnesses and 300 exhibits. Both sides can adjust how they present their evidence at the retrial.
The next jury is scheduled to begin taking shape on March 29.

PLYMOUTH — A judge on Monday set a March date for Lindsay Clancy’s retrial in the killings of her three children in 2023, as prosecutors indirectly suggested they’ll retry her on charges of first-degree murder.
Judge William F. Sullivan set the March 29 trial date during a hearing in Plymouth Superior Court, after pressing prosecutors for a decision on whether they plan to retry Clancy on first-degree murder charges.
Assistant District Attorney Jennifer Sprague said the Commonwealth “is ready to pick a jury trial date,” but declined to specify on what charges.
First-degree murder charges would require the empanelment of a second jury. If prosecutors pursue lesser charges of second-degree murder or manslaughter, then Clancy would be allowed to waive her right to a jury trial and face a trial before a judge.
“The die has been cast,” Clancy’s lawyer Kevin Reddington told the judge. “I think you can read between the lines that when they say that the case is going to require a jury, that it’s an indirect comment from the DA that they intend to proceed on first-degree murder indictments.”
Sullivan also set a Dec. 30 date to discuss pretrial issues in the case, and a Feb. 18 date for the final conference before the retrial.
“I feel bad for Lindsay,” Reddington told media as he left the courthouse. “I feel bad for her family. I feel bad for the jurors that haven’t been picked yet. I feel bad for everybody that has anything to do with this case.”
He added that the prospect of a retrial is very emotional and distressing, “but nevertheless, we’ve got to get it done and that’s why we pressed to have it done this spring.”
Still, he said the defense may have an advantage over prosecutors during the retrial “because we’ve already had a dry run. We know what their case is.”
Plymouth District Attorney Timothy J. Cruz, who has yet to announce whether he will retry Clancy on first-degree murder charges, did not attend Monday’s hearing. His office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Shortly after the hearing, attorney Martin G. Weinberg, one of Clancy’s lawyers, filed a petition with a single justice of the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court appealing Sullivan’s denial of a defense motion to dismiss the murder charges based on double jeopardy. He urged the justice to hold a hearing, then report the matter to the court’s seven-member bench for a ruling.
Reddington said he was not seeking a stay of the retrial while the petition is pending and expected the court would rule quickly on the matter.
Clancy, 36, admitted she strangled 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson, and 8-month-old Callan with exercise bands in the basement of their Duxbury home on Jan. 24, 2023, after sending her then-husband, Patrick, out to pick up medication and takeout for dinner.
She slashed her wrists and neck after killing the children and then jumped out of a second-story window, leaving her paralyzed from the waist down.
Clancy pleaded not guilty to three counts of first-degree murder, asserting that she should not be held criminally responsible because of mental illness; she claims she was suffering from postpartum psychosis after the birth of her third child and hallucinated a man’s voice commanding her to kill herself and the children.
Prosecutors argued that the slayings were premeditated by Clancy, who wanted to kill herself and her children because she was unhappy with her life.
In September, Sullivan declared a mistrial after jurors reported they were deadlocked 11-1 after a six-week trial, with all but one voting to find her not guilty by lack of criminal responsibility.
Clancy faces mandatory life in prison if convicted of first-degree murder charges. If acquitted based on insanity, she would be committed to a state psychiatric hospital, where she would remain while undergoing periodic evaluations by a judge to determine whether she could be released without posing a danger to the community.
During Monday’s hearing, Sullivan rejected Sprague’s request to delay Clancy’s trial until later in the year while the two prosecutors assigned to the case handle other cases that are slated for trial in the spring.
“This is a case that I want to get tried,” Sullivan said. “We’ve all done retrials and in general, the sooner a case is retried the better for all parties, including the attorneys, instead of waiting a year to get things done.”
Last week, Sullivan denied a defense motion to dismiss the charges against Clancy on double jeopardy grounds, rejecting claims that he improperly declared a mistrial and that it would be unconstitutional to try Clancy for the same grounds twice.
In a 55-page petition filed Monday with a single justice of the state’s highest court, Weinberg argued that Sullivan failed to conduct a meaningful after the jury foreperson sent notes during deliberations indicating that a holdout juror was failing to follow instructions regarding reasonable doubt.
At the time, Sullivan questioned each juror at sidebar about whether they were able to follow his instructions on the law, but denied a defense request to delve deeper, saying it wouldn’t be proper to intrude on jury deliberations. He denied a defense request to replace the juror with one of the alternates.
In Monday’s petition, Weinberg argued the judge could have questioned jurors specifically about their ability to follow his instructions regarding reasonable doubt without invading jury deliberations.
“The mere fact that the jury had reported a deadlock did not relieve the trial court of its obligation to investigate juror misconduct and ensure that the defendant received a fair trial,” Weinberg wrote.

Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother who argues she should not be held criminally responsible for killing her three children, is slated to face a second trial beginning on March 29, 2027, less than a year after her first trial ended with a hung jury.
Prosecutors said in court Monday the charges require a jury trial. That appeared to indicate they intend to retry Clancy on the same charges of first-degree murder, which requires a jury trial.
“The die has been cast,” defense attorney Kevin Reddington said. “I think you can read between the lines that when they say the case is going to require a jury, that it’s an indirect comment from the (District Attorney) that they intend to proceed on first-degree murder indictments.”
In her first trial, Clancy faced three counts of first-degree murder, though the jury was able to consider lesser charges in their deliberations. The judge declared a mistrial after the jury deadlocked, with one holdout juror preventing the panel from finding Clancy not guilty by lack of criminal responsibility.
Deciding on a trial date Monday led to some frustration among the prosecution, defense and judge, with the defense pushing for an earlier date and the prosecution concerned about the scheduling of other murder trials. The court also set pre-trial hearings for December 30 and February 18.
The prosecution’s decision to retry Clancy is the latest development in the triple-murder case that became one of the most debated criminal trials in recent memory this summer before it ended in a mistrial.

Legal experts cautioned the retrial is not set in stone and could be altered by prosecutorial decisions or plea negotiations before the start of the trial.
“Monday will be significant in that it would be a signal about the prosecution’s big picture decision about whether it wants to pursue criminal charges as opposed to dismissing them,” Daniel Medwed, a professor of law and criminal justice at Northeastern University School of Law, told CNN prior to Monday’s hearing.
“But what happens on Monday is the beginning, not the end, because a lot of different things could happen in the run-up to trial.”
Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz, who could initiate plea negotiations, did not appear in court Monday. CNN has reached out to his office for further information.
Outside court, Reddington said he did not believe a plea deal was possible. “I don’t think they’d give me the right time of day at this point,” he said.
Separately, Clancy’s defense filed an appeal Monday before the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court, asking it to overturn Judge William Sullivan’s ruling rejecting her motion to dismiss the charges – a decision that paved the way for the retrial.
Clancy’s attorneys have argued, in part, that a retrial would violate her constitutional protections against double jeopardy.
What happened at the first trial
Clancy’s trial this summer featured emotional testimony from her ex-husband, Patrick, family members and friends, Clancy’s doctors and psychiatric experts.
The prosecution argued that Clancy’s actions before the killings, including sending her husband out of the house on errands, show she knew what she was doing when she killed her children.
In contrast, Clancy has said in court filings and interviews with psychiatric experts that she heard a male voice directing her to kill her children and then herself and lost control of her actions.
The case put a spotlight on maternal mental health, postpartum psychosis, the internet’s tendency toward conspiracy and the ongoing skepticism of the so-called “insanity defense.”
After more than a month of testimony, the 12-person jury was unable to come to a unanimous decision due to a lone holdout juror. Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial due to the deadlock, setting up the possibility of a retrial with a new jury.

Jurors said a lone juror refused to join 11 others in finding Clancy not guilty of murder.

When deliberations were dragging out at the end of the trial, Reddington had asked the judge to remove the holdout juror, saying the jury foreperson reported one juror refused to follow the law in regards to reasonable doubt. Sullivan declined to dismiss the juror, saying he reaffirmed his instructions with all the jurors about the law.

Clancy, 36, did not testify during the trial. But her attorneys didn't deny that she killed her three children in January of 2023. "I'm appalled and disgusted," Reddington said of Clancy's medical care, as NPR and WBUR reported. "It's repulsive what happened here."
But prosecutors argued Clancy was mentally capable of committing a premeditated crime, accusing her of sending her husband out on errands so she would be alone with their children. And they raised doubts about Clancy's claims that a voice told her to kill them.
"This case is not about our mental health system or how it treats women," Assistant District Attorney Jennifer Sprague said in her closing statement. "That's a distraction to get you angry and passionate about an important issue, but an issue that's not on trial here."
During the trial, the jury visited the house where the Clancy children died. Their bus route also took them past two places Patrick Clancy visited that evening — a CVS and a takeout restaurant -- before returning home to a horrific scene. Sullivan told the jurors that the visit, called a "view" under Massachusetts state law, was meant to "help you better understand the evidence" by seeing the locations and the house's layout.

PLYMOUTH, Mass. — Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother who argues she should not be held criminally responsible for killing her three children, is slated to face a second trial beginning on March 29, 2027, less than a year after her first trial ended with a hung jury.
Prosecutors said in court the case would require a jury trial, an indication they intend to retry Clancy on the same charges of first-degree murder.
In her first trial, Clancy faced three counts of first-degree murder, though the jury was able to consider lesser charges in their deliberations. The judge declared a mistrial after the jury deadlocked, with one holdout juror preventing the panel from finding Clancy not guilty by lack of criminal responsibility.
Deciding on a trial date led to some frustration among the prosecution, defense and judge, with the defense pushing for an earlier date and the prosecution concerned about the scheduling of other murder trials. The court also set pre-trial hearings for December 30 and February 18, 2027.
The prosecution's decision to retry Clancy is the latest development in the triple-murder case that became one of the most debated criminal trials in recent memory this summer before it ended in a mistrial.
Prosecutors have argued Clancy, 36, "acted intentionally, rationally and swiftly" when she fatally strangled her three children in their Duxbury home and attempted suicide in January 2023. Her defense argued she was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time and should not be held criminally responsible for the deaths of Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and 8-month-old Callan.
Legal experts cautioned the retrial is not set in stone and could be altered by prosecutorial decisions or plea negotiations before the start of the trial.
"Monday will be significant in that it would be a signal about the prosecution's big picture decision about whether it wants to pursue criminal charges as opposed to dismissing them," said Daniel Medwed, a professor of law and criminal justice at Northeastern University School of Law.
"But what happens on Monday is the beginning, not the end, because a lot of different things could happen in the run-up to trial."
What happened at the first trial
Clancy's trial this summer featured emotional testimony from her ex-husband, Patrick, family members and friends, Clancy's doctors and psychiatric experts. The case put a spotlight on maternal mental health, postpartum psychosis, the internet's tendency toward conspiracy and the ongoing skepticism of the so-called "insanity defense."
After more than a month of testimony, the 12-person jury was unable to come to a unanimous decision due to a lone holdout juror. Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial due to the deadlock, setting up the possibility of a retrial with a new jury.

She could face life in prison if convicted of murder. If jurors find she cannot be held criminally responsible, the court will likely begin the process of committing her to a psychiatric hospital.
Since the mistrial, Reddington filed a series of motions seeking to prevent a retrial, but Sullivan rejected each of them in turn.
In a retrial, the case starts over with a new jury, prosecutors and the defense make their arguments and witnesses take the stand and testify. In general, a retrial can be quite similar to the original trial, although the parties may drop weaker arguments and focus more on their stronger evidence.

Following the killings, Clancy attempted to take her own life by jumping from a second-story window, leaving her partially paralyzed. She survived and was subsequently charged in connection with her children’s deaths.
Throughout her first trial, the defense maintained that Clancy was experiencing postpartum psychosis, a severe psychiatric condition that can occur after childbirth. Her attorneys argued that her mental illness prevented her from being criminally responsible for her actions.

Clancy’s legal team immediately challenged that outcome, arguing the judge should have investigated the lone holdout juror before ending the proceedings.
Her attorneys maintained that the circumstances surrounding the jury’s deadlock raised questions about whether a second prosecution would violate her constitutional protection against double jeopardy, which generally prevents someone from being prosecuted twice after a final acquittal or conviction for the same offense.
However, on November 9, Sullivan rejected the defense’s attempt to dismiss the charges. He determined that the jury’s inability to agree justified declaring a mistrial and that another trial would not violate Clancy’s constitutional rights.

A conviction on first-degree murder charges in Massachusetts carries a mandatory sentence of life imprisonment without the possibility of parole.
